threat_assessment:
Three players decided what you are before you untapped on turn three. Howling Mine, Temple Bell, a Rabbit handing out free cards — that reads as a player who wants a long, friendly game, and nobody spends removal on a long, friendly game. That read is the most valuable thing you own. Spend it on purpose, because it runs out.

Start with what you are actually handing across the table. Kwain, Itinerant Meddler and The Second Doctor do not give cards away — they present a choice where both answers pay you. You cannot aim the Doctor's end-step offer, so sell it: talk the widest board into taking the card, because whoever accepts cannot attack you or your permanents next turn. That rider guards all four of your walkers, and it costs you a card you were happy to give.

Every accepted card also walks a hand toward seven, which is where Ebony Owl Netsuke charges 4 and Iron Maiden charges hand size minus four — stack 003 walks that upkeep to exactly 7 damage. So push the gifts at whoever sits closest to the threshold, and land them before that player's upkeep begins. A card handed over during their upkeep is just a card.

Here is the part pilots get wrong: deflection is a budget, and yours spends down every time the engine shows itself (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection). Five moments spend it. Choose each one instead of stumbling into it.

One — engine and punisher visible together. That pairing lands by turn six in 41.2% of games, so the turn it does, stop adding to that side of the board. You have a clock now, and a clock wants you holding mana, not deploying into three opponents.

Two — Forced Fruition resolving. It is the loudest permanent you own and it dresses itself up as an apology. Cast it when the table's answers are already spent, never as your opening statement.

Three — Heliod flipped with cards in hand. He is down by turn six in 90.2% of games, and from that turn every untapped land you leave reads as a counterspell. Bank the misread: leave two up on the turns you hold nothing and let the table play around a card you do not have.

Four — Aetherflux Reservoir sitting beside Hullbreaker Horror. Anyone who has done the reading solves stack 006 on sight and turns the pod's whole removal suite toward your seat. Deploy the Reservoir last, on the commit turn itself, never a turn early to develop. Sol Ring and Arcane Signet are furniture, the Horror is a flash blocker with a bounce trigger, and the Reservoir is the confession.

Five — an end-step Enlightened Tutor after the midgame. That is your scheduler, so use it as one: fire it on the right-hand opponent's end step and your draw step delivers the fourth piece, and the commit turn opens without the table ever having seen a three-of-four board. It is a tell in reverse, too. Early it reads as value — a punisher, a tax piece, a doubler. Late and at an end step it reads as their untap is the go turn, so run that version behind open counter mana.

The commit turn is this deck's real skill test, and the sequencing is strict. Cast Grand Abolisher as the first spell of the go turn, not the turn before. A shield left standing through a full rotation is an announcement, and three players will answer it — or you — at sorcery speed with three players' worth of resources.

Lead with him and he does three jobs at once. The static shuts every window for the rest of your turn. He is cast number one on the ledger, because the Reservoir counts every spell you have cast this turn. And the only interactable moment left is the response to Abolisher himself, while every piece that matters is still in your hand.

Be as honest about the windows as stack 006 is. Without the Abolisher, all fifteen casts and all three activations hand priority to three opponents, and nothing in the engine closes any of them. Instant speed is what kills you: a counter on a loop rock, artifact removal mid-ledger, a damage redirect on an activation while the ledger has you at 3 life. Count the open blue mana before you begin, not after cast six.

Two things beat the line with no window at all, and the Abolisher touches neither. A cast-limit static ends a fifteen-cast turn where it stands, and a per-spell tax breaks the mana neutrality that stacks 004 and 005 pinned down — a loop that is not neutral is not a loop. Scan for both before you commit; those are the boards where you wait a turn and win anyway. Channel lands are the third gap: a card in hand is not an artifact, a creature or an enchantment, so respect the seat holding one untapped land and a full grip.

Do not reach for Teferi's Protection as a combo shield. Your life total cannot change while it is up and your own board phases out, so it cannot share a turn with a ledger that pays 50 life three times. Hold it for the swing back, or for the wrath that catches you tapped low. It is the card that buys back the turn you spent becoming the archenemy — keep it for that job and nothing else.

Drannith Magistrate carries political weight out of all proportion to a small body. Cast into a fresh pod on turn two, it unites three commander-dependent players against you for no return. Cast when one commander is already the table's shared problem, and two opponents will defend it for you (strategy:multiplayer.politics). Sell it as the answer to their problem, and never promise anyone a commander lock the record has not verified — it stops casting, and that is all it stops.

There is exactly one board where you should let the Reservoir show early. The punisher clock is already public, upkeeps are bleeding around the table, and you are holding free interaction, which the sim has by turn six in 67.2% of games. On that board a visible Reservoir soaks the artifact removal that would otherwise take Iron Maiden, and the fear freezes a table that is already losing life for free. Every other early Reservoir is a donation you did not mean to make.

Set your own expiry date on being nice. Access to a win condition arrives by turn six in 50.5% of games and in 61.2% overall, so treat the quiet plan as a phase rather than a personality. The turn the tutor schedules the fourth piece behind an Abolisher, stop playing fair and take the game. You have already been paid for every card you gave away.
matchups:
One question sorts every table you will sit at: can these three decks use the cards you are handing them? Answer it before the first Mine hits the battlefield. Your generosity is matchup-dependent; your punishers never are.

Against sweeper control and in the mirror, somebody has to be the beatdown and it is not you (strategy:whos-the-beatdown). The punisher clock advances while both of you draw-go, so let it advance and refuse to spend first. Every optional card you hand a control deck comes back as an answer — keep Kwain untapped against the seat with open blue and let the symmetric draw engines carry the hands upward instead.

Then use the reset they cannot counter. Supreme Verdict clears their board through open permission, and Jace Beleren, Jace Wielder of Mysteries, Teferi Temporal Pilgrim and Teferi Hero of Dominaria all survive it in both directions (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math). Buy resilience and wrath freely — you are trading their creatures for none of yours.

Build your turns around Teferi, Hero of Dominaria in this matchup. The +1 draws and untaps two lands at the next end step, so your clock ticks while your counter mana stays open, and the -3 tucks the one permanent they cannot rebuy. Take Archmage's Charm's draw-two mode in a permission standoff rather than holding a dead card, and steal their Sol Ring when the game turns on rocks.

Creature wraths barely touch you — the sim puts 1.5 bodies on your board at turn six — with one exception you cannot afford. Hullbreaker Horror is a combo piece, never a blocker. Do not flash it in as value against a control seat; a wrath that eats it costs you the verified kill, not a seven-drop.

Your real exposure is one Farewell-class card taking the Mines, the punishers and the Reservoir together. Deploy in layers and never show both punishers and the Reservoir to the same board state. The piece you have not fetched is the piece nobody can sweep, so leave it in the library and let Enlightened Tutor collect it on the end step you choose.

Stax and tax attack the one thing this deck needs: several cheap spells in a turn. Recount your hand under the tax before you sequence anything, and assume the real number is one lower than it looks (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial). Under an assembling lock you are the beatdown, so decide quickly.

Most of it you simply outrun. The kill asks for four cards and {2} to begin, so a soft lock that does not tax artifact casts is a lock you race, and Enlightened Tutor buys the missing piece for one white mana through a starved board.

Know the two pieces you cannot outrun. A cast-limit effect caps the fifteen-cast turn where it sits, and a per-spell tax breaks the loop's mana neutrality. Answer the second lock piece, not the first inconvenience — a lone tax creature is an annoyance, a tax plus a cast limit is a funeral.

Teferi, Hero of Dominaria is the workhorse here too. Tuck a lock piece third from the top with the -3, where indestructible and totem armor mean nothing, and claw mana back with the +1's untap under a Winter Orb-class effect. Blink Loran of the Third Path with Displacer Kitten for a repeatable artifact answer, and remember you are half a prison deck yourself — Drannith Magistrate turns off every commander-dependent seat and flips the lock around.

Then take the rebate nobody else gets. Heliod's discount grows with every card your opponents drew this turn, so under a Sphere-class tax you should be more generous, not less: tap Kwain, run the Mines, and buy your turn back at a price the stax player cannot charge you for.

Aggro is where your gifts can kill you, because an aggressive deck empties its hand and your Mines refill it. Never lead with Forced Fruition into that pod. Land Iron Maiden or Ebony Owl Netsuke first so the refill arrives taxed — stack 003 walks it: hands over seven pay, cleanup trims to exactly seven, and the damage lands before the cards get spent.

Make yourself the worst attack at the table. Propaganda charges 2 per creature swinging your way, and The Second Doctor's rider takes a whole combat step from anyone who accepts his card, walkers included. One card blanking three attack plans is what virtual card advantage looks like in multiplayer (strategy:card-advantage.virtual), so talk the widest board into taking the draw every end step.

Commit little and hold Supreme Verdict. With 1.5 bodies on board at turn six you are not blocking your way out of this — you are absorbing until the reset is worth casting, and the punishers get paid the entire time.

Count your life total as a combo resource in this matchup. Stack 006's fifteen-cast minimum is computed from 32 life, and the requirement scales: the casts have to gain 151 minus whatever you are at, so 20 life makes it 16 casts and 8 life makes it 17. Every extra cast is another open priority window. Take Kwain's free life, treat every point of chip damage as disruption, and go a turn earlier rather than a window longer.

Against combo, be the disciplined one — you have both the tools and the numbers. Free or cheap interaction is in your hand by turn six in 67.2% of games, so spend it only on the card that ends the game (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy). Countering a ramp spell is how you die holding a Force of Negation.

Give a storm deck nothing. Kwain stays untapped, the Doctor's offer gets sold to the other two seats, and Forced Fruition stays in your hand unless a punisher is already down and you are the one about to win. Seven cards per spell is their dream turn and your obituary.

Land Drannith Magistrate early against a graveyard- or command-zone-driven line and let it eat the removal earmarked for your kill. Know its limit before you tap out: it stops casting from anywhere but hand, which blanks flashback, escape and cast-from-exile, and it does nothing to a reanimation spell that puts a creature onto the battlefield without casting it.

Then out-combo them. Enlightened Tutor is an instant, so hold interaction and assemble on the same turn — tutor at the end step before your untap. With a checker-passed kill behind a Grand Abolisher you are often the fastest deck in the pod, and the fastest deck does not durdle (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window).

Graveyard decks and incidental hate should not frighten you at all. Your own graveyard use is one delve spell and a Torrential Gearhulk target, so a Rest in Peace costs you a card of value and never touches the Hullbreaker kill. Do not counter it — counter the thing that recurs. Against that seat Drannith Magistrate is your best card, your counters are the backup, and their game-ending spell usually arrives early enough that the free interaction is already in your hand.

Whatever sits across from you, the shape of the plan does not move. Give away cards that cost them more than they cost you, price the gifts with a punisher, and hold the four pieces until the turn you can spend them all at once. You are the one collecting.
how_it_wins:
The table has you filed under "the nice one." Howling Mine, Font of Mythos, Temple Bell, Kami of the Crescent Moon, Dictate of Kruphix, Folio of Fancies, Kwain and The Second Doctor all read as gifts, and Forced Fruition reads as an apology. Play into that. You are charging for every card you hand out, three separate ways, and none of the invoices arrive on the turn the gift does.

Heliod is the hinge, and he is a turn-four card: the sim casts him by turn six in 90.2% of games, median turn four. Front face rebuys an enchantment. The flip is what you actually want — everything you own gains flash, and your spells cost {1} less for each card your opponents drew this turn. So flip on a turn the Mines have already fired, and let the table's generosity pay your mana bill while you hold counters.

The kill is four cards and one main phase: Hullbreaker Horror, Sol Ring, Arcane Signet, Aetherflux Reservoir. Stack 006 walks the whole thing. The loop breaks exactly even on mana, so your cast count has no ceiling, and the Reservoir turns each cast into life — cast n pays n. From 32 life, fifteen casts is the floor: 53 life buys the first 50-damage activation, 60 buys the second, 52 buys the third, and you finish at 2 with the table empty.

Respect what the same artifact costs you. Every cast and every activation in that sequence hands three opponents an open window, and the Horror protects none of it. Grand Abolisher is the answer the record names — lay him the turn before, or lead the go-turn with him. Failing that, hold the counter you drew; the sim has cheap or free interaction in hand by turn six in 67.2% of games.

Plan B is cleaner and slower. Approach of the Second Sun gains 7 and buries itself seventh from the top — nothing, in a deck where the whole table draws in bulk and two doublers accelerate your digging. Mystical Tutor or Long-Term Plans puts it straight back. Stack 002 verified the second cast end to end: cast it with counter mana up, because the stack is the only place they can touch it.

Plan C runs whether you tap out or not. Iron Maiden and Viseling charge hand size minus four at every opponent's upkeep; Ebony Owl Netsuke charges a flat 4 at seven cards. Stack 003 verified the arithmetic — a punished hand trims to exactly seven at cleanup, then takes 4 and 3 the next upkeep, and you spent nothing. The two-piece only assembles by turn six in 41.2% of games, so plan on being the control deck most of the time. That is not the consolation prize. That is the deck you are good at, right up to the turn the fourth kill piece lands behind an Abolisher.

combo_lines.001: The clause is CR 603.3c: a modal trigger's mode is announced when the ability goes on the stack, and "if one of the modes would be illegal... that mode can't be chosen." At that moment the Sol Ring that caused the trigger is a spell you control — not a spell you don't control, and not a permanent, which CR 110.1 puts on the battlefield only. The holding: this pair loops nothing. The trigger can never reach the card that made it — too early while it is a spell, already gone once it is a permanent.
combo_lines.002: Both clauses here are about time. Approach's condition asks whether you have cast another spell with that name this game — an event in the record, not a property of any card — so shuffling the first copy back into the library erases nothing. And the win is an instruction followed during resolution under CR 608.2c, not a state-based action. The holding: their one window is while the second copy sits on the stack, and Swan Song contests it there. Once all players pass, nobody has priority again and the game ends mid-resolution.
combo_lines.003: The clause is CR 603.3: a triggered ability goes on the stack above the spell that triggered it. Forced Fruition's trigger therefore resolves before the Naturalize aimed at it, and CR 113.7a keeps an ability alive after its source dies. They draw the seven either way. Cleanup then trims them to exactly seven — the number Ebony Owl Netsuke's intervening "if" is looking for. The holding: removal does not cancel draws already owed. Both upkeep triggers are yours to order, and here the order changes nothing: 4 and 3, seven damage.
combo_lines.004: The distinction CR 110.1 draws — a permanent is on the battlefield, a spell is not — is exactly what the three-card version has and the two-card version lacks. Sol Ring is already on the battlefield, so it is an appropriate target for the trigger the Signet's cast creates. It is tapped while that trigger is pending; the bounce resolves; the recast produces the trigger that returns the Signet. One full cycle: three mana spent, three produced. The holding: the cast count is unbounded inside a main phase, and the loop yields nothing else — no mana, no cards, no damage. Thought Vessel substitutes exactly.
combo_lines.005: The petition is that Displacer Kitten's blink turns the even cycle mana-positive. Denied, on two clauses that interlock: a trigger's targets are locked when it is put on the stack (CR 603.3d), and a permanent that changes zones returns as a new object (CR 400.7). Whichever trigger resolves first makes the other's target illegal, and the second does not resolve. The holding: bounce and blink can never both land on one cast. On the loop-preserving ordering the Kitten adds nothing; on the blink-first ordering the entire gain is one terminal float of three mana, and the loop ends there.
combo_lines.006: Start with what the record says the Reservoir's activation is not: an ability on the stack is not a card, so it is not a spell (CR 112.1), and the Horror never triggers on it. Everything else holds. Unbounded casts feed "gain 1 life for each spell you've cast this turn" — cast n pays n, so k casts pay k(k+1)/2 — and from 32 life, fifteen casts is the proven minimum to fund three activations, each killing by state-based action under CR 704.5a. The holding: the kill is complete off these four cards and {2}, and every cast and every activation opens a real priority window that nothing in the engine closes.

card_roles.Heliod, the Radiant Dawn // Heliod, the: The front face rebuys an enchantment on arrival; the flip is the card you actually want, granting everything flash and shaving {1} per card your opponents drew this turn. Flip on a turn the Mines have already fired, not the turn you cast him.
card_roles.Aetherflux Reservoir: The kill's cashier: every cast gains 1 life per spell you've cast this turn, and 50 life buys 50 damage at any target. Deploy it last, after the loop pieces are down, because it is the piece that tells the table what you are doing.
card_roles.Alhammarret's Archive: Doubles your draws and your life gain and nobody else's — the most asymmetric card in a deck full of symmetric ones. Get it down before you start handing out cards, not after.
card_roles.An Offer You Can't Refuse: One mana stops any noncreature spell and hands them two Treasures. Great on your go-turn when nothing after it matters; poor on turn three, when the Treasures fund the exact thing you were afraid of.
card_roles.Approach of the Second Sun: Plan B, and a clean one: the first cast gains 7 and buries it seventh from the top, which is nothing in a deck where everyone draws in bulk. Cast the second with counter mana up — the stack is the only place they can answer it.
card_roles.Arcane Denial: Counters anything for two, they draw two, you draw one. Point it at the spell that ends the game, never at ramp — you are paying for this in their cards.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Either colour off two mana, and the exact second rock the verified loop runs on. Thought Vessel does the same job in the loop, so you have two — spend the first freely and keep track of the second.
card_roles.Azorius Signet: Two mana in, {W}{U} out for a {1} activation. It is the card that turns a blue hand white; cast it on turn two, where it converts into a turn-three Heliod.
card_roles.Braingeyser: X cards to any player. Aim it at yourself to dig for a kill piece, or at the opponent whose upkeep Iron Maiden is about to charge for.
card_roles.Consecrated Sphinx: Two cards every time any opponent draws one — in a deck that makes them draw constantly, this is the best thing you can resolve. Expect it to eat the table's first removal spell, and be happy about it.
card_roles.Counterspell: Two blue, counter anything, no strings. Save it for the go-turn window rather than spending it on the first scary permanent you see.
card_roles.Cyclonic Rift: Instant-speed bounce for two, or {6}{U} to clear every nonland permanent you don't control. Overload it as the shield on your kill turn, not as a midgame tempo swing.
card_roles.Dictate of Kruphix: Everyone draws an extra card each turn — three extra hands a lap, pushing three opponents toward the Netsuke's seven. Flash means you never have to tap low on your own turn to deploy it.
card_roles.Dig Through Time: Delve makes it cheap in a deck whose graveyard fills with spent counterspells. Two cards from seven, at instant speed: use it to find the missing kill piece, not to refill a full hand.
card_roles.Displacer Kitten: Every noncreature cast blinks a permanent you control — Mystic Remora returns with no age counters, Loran re-fires its removal. Do not try to bolt it onto the Hullbreaker loop; stack 005 refuted that line.
card_roles.Dovin's Veto: Two mana, can't be countered, stops any noncreature spell. This is the one you hold for the counter-war over your own go-turn.
card_roles.Drannith Magistrate: Two mana that shuts opponents out of their commanders, graveyards and exile. It will die — so play it on the turn you need the lock, not simply on curve.
card_roles.Ebony Owl Netsuke: A flat 4 to any opponent sitting on seven or more cards at their upkeep. Below seven it does nothing at all, so it only comes online behind the Mines.
card_roles.Faerie Mastermind: A flash flier that draws you a card whenever an opponent draws their second in a turn — which, with a Mine out, is everyone every turn. The {3}{U} activation is a Kwain you already control.
card_roles.Fierce Guardianship: A free counter as long as Heliod is on the battlefield. It is the cheapest way to protect a go-turn, but it is not interaction in an opening hand — it is interaction from turn five.
card_roles.Folio of Fancies: Nobody has a maximum hand size, so the cleanup trim your punishers rely on stops happening — which is upside, because the Maiden's number keeps climbing. The {X}{X} activation is your force-feed button.
card_roles.Font of Mythos: Two extra cards per player per draw step: the fastest route to three seven-card hands. It also arms whoever at the table uses cards best, so read the room before you deploy it.
card_roles.Force of Negation: Free on other players' turns if you exile a blue card, and it exiles what it counters. Keep it for the turn somebody else tries to win.
card_roles.Forced Fruition: The centrepiece: every spell an opponent casts hands that player seven cards. Stack 003 verified they draw the seven even when the spell they cast is the removal that kills it — it pays for itself on the way out.
card_roles.Grand Abolisher: Two white mana that closes every window your kill turn opens: on your turn, opponents can't cast spells or activate abilities of artifacts, creatures or enchantments. Lay him the turn before, or lead the go-turn with him.
card_roles.Howling Mine: Everyone draws one more; you charge for it three ways. Cheap and early — the first Mine is what starts the punisher clock ticking.
card_roles.Hullbreaker Horror: The engine's heart: uncounterable, flash, and every spell you cast bounces a permanent or a spell you don't control. Flash him in on somebody's end step, then untap into the loop.
card_roles.Iron Maiden: Damage equal to hand size minus four at every opponent's upkeep — all three of them, every lap, for free. Against normal hands it is nothing, so don't burn a turn-three slot on it before an engine exists.
card_roles.Jace Beleren: The +2 gives everyone a card, which is precisely the trade this deck wins: three punisher triggers' worth of fuel plus your own discount. Treat him as a Howling Mine with loyalty to spare, not as an ultimate.
card_roles.Jace, Wielder of Mysteries: A standing win condition that draws while it waits — empty library, you win instead of losing. With two draw doublers in the 99 that is a real clock, not a curiosity.
card_roles.Kami of the Crescent Moon: Two mana, everyone draws an extra card every turn, and it blocks. Play it into an empty board; it is the cheapest engine you have.
card_roles.Kwain, Itinerant Meddler: Tap for a table-wide optional draw and a life each. The point is that opponents almost always say yes, and every yes is Maiden math plus your discount.
card_roles.Leyline of Anticipation: Free from your opening hand, four mana otherwise. Keep the opener that has it — flash on everything is how you hold counters and still develop.
card_roles.Long-Term Plans: Finds any card in the deck and buries it third from the top, which with the Mines running is a turn away. This is how the last kill piece or the second Approach arrives on schedule.
card_roles.Loran of the Third Path: An enters-the-battlefield trigger that kills an artifact or enchantment, plus a tap that draws you and one opponent a card. With Displacer Kitten out, that removal trigger stops being a one-shot.
card_roles.Mathemagics: Doubling X cards to any player — an absurd number at five or six mana. It is a sorcery, so under the Warped Eclipse or a Leyline it becomes an end-step force-feed instead of a main-phase one.
card_roles.Metallurgic Summonings: Every instant or sorcery you cast leaves behind a Construct the size of that spell, which is how a draw-go deck ends up with blockers it never spent a card on. The exile ability rebuys your whole spent counter suite.
card_roles.Mystic Remora: One mana that taxes the entire table for three or four turns. Pay the cumulative upkeep while it draws, and let it go the turn the payment would cost you your counter mana.
card_roles.Mystical Tutor: One mana, instant speed, any instant or sorcery to the top — including the second Approach (stack 002). Cast it on the end step before your turn so the card arrives on your draw.
card_roles.Path to Exile: One mana exiles any creature and they get a basic. Spend it on the thing that kills you, not on the thing that annoys you.
card_roles.Pearl Medallion: Every white spell costs {1} less. Small, and small is the difference between holding Swords to Plowshares and holding Swords plus a counter.
card_roles.Propaganda: Attacking you costs {2} a creature. It won't stop a determined board, but it buys the turns the punisher clock needs, and turns are the entire point of a fort.
card_roles.Prosperity: Everyone draws X. Pick the X that pushes three hands past seven, then let the punishers collect on the way around the table — and you drew the same X.
card_roles.Psychosis Crawler: Its size is your hand size, and every card you draw drains each opponent for one. With two draw doublers running, that number gets embarrassing without you doing anything.
card_roles.Rhystic Study: The tax that decides games: they pay {1} or you draw. The card is worth exactly as much as your willingness to ask every single time.
card_roles.Sapphire Medallion: Blue spells cost {1} less, and 40 cards here carry a blue pip. It does not touch the loop's colourless rocks — stack 004 says so — so judge it purely as curve smoothing.
card_roles.Scrawling Crawler: Draws the table a card on your upkeep and drains each opponent one for every card they draw. It is the punisher that scales with your Mines instead of their hand size.
card_roles.Skyscribing: Everyone draws X, and the forecast drips one card a turn to the table straight from your hand. Use the forecast on the turns you must keep counter mana open.
card_roles.Smothering Tithe: Every opposing draw is {2} from them or a Treasure for you, in a deck that makes them draw two and three at a time. Read it as a ramp spell wearing a tax's clothes.
card_roles.Sol Ring: The best turn-one play in the deck and a verified loop piece besides. On a turn the kill is live, do not spend it on anything marginal.
card_roles.Sphinx's Tutelage: Every draw you make mills an opponent two, chaining on colour matches, and you draw a lot. Treat it as free progress on a third axis, never as the plan.
card_roles.Stroke of Genius: Instant-speed X cards to any player. At yourself it digs; at an opponent it force-feeds a hand into Iron Maiden range at exactly the moment you choose.
card_roles.Supreme Verdict: An uncounterable wipe that all four of your planeswalkers live through. Cast it when the table has committed and you have not — that asymmetry is the whole card.
card_roles.Swan Song: One mana counters an enchantment, instant or sorcery, and they get a 2/2 flier. Hold it for their counterspell; stack 002 walks that exact exchange over the second Approach.
card_roles.Swords to Plowshares: One mana exiles any creature and they gain the life. The life is irrelevant next to the tempo — spend it on a commander, never on a token.
card_roles.Talisman of Progress: Either colour for a point of damage, colourless for free. Two-mana rocks are how this deck gets Heliod down on turn three, so cast it on two.
card_roles.Teferi's Ageless Insight: Doubles every draw after your first each turn, and it stacks with Alhammarret's Archive. Once one of these lands, your own Mines are drawing you two and three a turn.
card_roles.Teferi's Protection: Three mana: your life can't change, you gain protection from everything, and your board phases out. It answers a wrath, an alpha strike and somebody else's table-kill with one card — so hold it rather than cycling it for tempo.
card_roles.Teferi, Temporal Pilgrim: Gains a loyalty counter on every card you draw, which in this deck is several a turn cycle. The 0 draws, and the -2 leaves a Spirit that grows every time you draw too.
card_roles.Temple Bell: Tap it and everyone draws — and unlike the Mines, you choose the moment. The end step before a punished opponent's upkeep is when that choice is worth the most.
card_roles.The Second Doctor: No maximum hand size for anyone, plus an end-step draw that blanks the acceptor's next attack against you. They keep the cards, and the cards are exactly what your punishers charge for.
card_roles.Thought Vessel: No maximum hand size for you, one colourless mana, and the substitute the verified loop accepts for Arcane Signet. Two loop-legal rocks is redundancy you should protect.
card_roles.Torrential Gearhulk: Flash in a 5/6 and free-cast an instant from your graveyard — with a yard full of spent counters, that is a two-for-one at the worst possible moment for them.
card_roles.Viseling: Hand size minus four at each opponent's upkeep, on a body this time. A second Iron Maiden, with the same rule: inert until the table is drawing extra.
card_roles.Teferi, Hero of Dominaria: The +1 draws and untaps two lands at the next end step — a clock that advances while your counter mana stays open, which is the posture this deck wants. The -3 tucks any nonland permanent, including the stax piece nothing else here answers.
card_roles.Archmage's Charm: Counter, draw two, or steal a mana-value-one permanent — it is never a dead card. It is also the only {U}{U}{U} in the deck, so plan it as a turn-four spell off duals rather than a turn-three promise.
card_roles.Enlightened Tutor: One white mana at instant speed for any artifact or enchantment: that is every kill piece except Hullbreaker himself, plus both punishers and Forced Fruition. Cast it on the end step before your go-turn so the piece lands on your draw.
card_roles.Island: Fourteen of them, and blue is the colour you cannot afford to be short on. When a keep is close, count Islands first.
card_roles.Plains: Only three, and with Eiganjo they are the only white-only mana here. Get one down early if your hand is holding Swords to Plowshares or Grand Abolisher.
card_roles.Adarkar Wastes: Both colours untapped for a point of damage, or colourless for free. Take the damage on the early turns and stop taking it once the Reservoir arithmetic starts to matter.
card_roles.Ancient Tomb: Two mana on turn one for two life — this is the card that puts Heliod down on turn three. Take the damage; you are the deck that gains it back.
card_roles.Command Tower: Both colours, untapped, no cost, no decision. Play it and move on.
card_roles.Deserted Beach: Untapped once you control two other lands, which means turn three onward. Lead on it only when the turn has nothing to cast anyway.
card_roles.Eiganjo, Seat of the Empire: A Plains that doubles as a removal spell you discard for, and the channel cost drops for each legendary creature you control. It is never a dead draw.
card_roles.Flooded Strand: A Plains or an Island for one life. Crack it on their end step, and take the white source if you are sitting on Grand Abolisher.
card_roles.Glacial Fortress: Untapped as long as you already control a Plains or an Island, and 17 of your lands are basics. Sequence a basic first and this is never a tapland.
card_roles.Hallowed Fountain: Two life for both colours untapped. Pay on the turns that matter; take the tapped land on the turns that don't.
card_roles.Irrigated Farmland: This one always enters tapped, and it cycles for {2} when you are flooded. Put it down on your cheapest turn.
card_roles.Mana Confluence: Any colour, a life a tap. It is what lets an all-blue hand cast Grand Abolisher, and the life is the smallest of your problems.
card_roles.Mikokoro, Center of the Sea: A colourless land that becomes "each player draws a card" for {2}. Fire it on the end step before a punished opponent's upkeep.
card_roles.Otawara, Soaring City: An Island that channels from your hand to bounce an artifact, creature, enchantment or planeswalker, cheaper for each legendary creature you control. Hold it when the answer is worth more than the land drop.
card_roles.Prairie Stream: Untapped once two basics are down — which is the sequencing tell for this whole base: basics first, duals second.
card_roles.Seachrome Coast: Untapped only while you control two or fewer other lands, so it is a turn-one or turn-two land. Later than that, expect it tapped and plan the turn around it.
card_roles.Skycloud Expanse: Both colours for {1} and a tap. A fine turn-five land and a poor turn-two one.
card_roles.Temple of Enlightenment: Always tapped, always scries. Spend it on the turn you weren't going to use all your mana anyway.
card_roles.Fellwar Stone: In the sideboard, and the only card there with a checker-passed verdict attached: stack 004 proves it runs the loop while an opponent controls a land that makes coloured mana, and proves it doesn't against empty boards.
card_roles.Vision Skeins: In the sideboard. Two cards to each opponent at instant speed — six drawn, a fat Heliod discount, three hands closer to seven — and it casts mid-counter-war, which none of your permanent engines can do.
card_roles.Ghostly Prison: In the sideboard, waiting for a pod with two or more combat seats. Alongside Propaganda and The Second Doctor's rider it blanks whole attack steps; against a draw-go table it is the deadest card you own.
card_roles.No More Lies: In the sideboard for fast-combo pods, where your symmetric engines are fuel for somebody else's turn. A {W}{U} tax counter that exiles beats recursion in a way your other counters don't.
card_roles.Sphinx of the Final Word: In the sideboard for heavy-permission tables: your instants and sorceries can't be countered, which closes the one window stack 002 leaves open on the second Approach. It does nothing for the Reservoir line — that kill is artifacts and an activation.
card_roles.Monastery Mentor: In the sideboard, and the deck's open question. Every cast in the verified loop is a noncreature spell, so the Monk count is arbitrarily large — but no stack scenario has walked whether a haste-less army beats the same-turn kill.
card_roles.Blue Sun's Zenith: In the sideboard with two live modes: X at yourself toward the Jace, Wielder finish, or X at a punished opponent's end step to force-feed Iron Maiden. The empty-library line has not been walked through yet.

mulligan:
Everyone mulligans this deck wrong the first time. It looks like a machine with a lot of moving parts, so the instinct is to dig for parts. Don't. The sim keeps 73.8% of first sevens and averages 0.33 mulligans a game, because the bar is three things: two to four lands, one card that draws, one card that says no.

Twenty-one of your spells cost two and nine cost one, so a two-land hand with a rock is a real hand, not a gamble. Keep Ancient Tomb plus a two-mana rock every time; that is the fast draw, and 27.7% of games have Heliod down by turn three. A table draw engine shows up by turn six in 75.4% of games, mean turn 2.5, so you do not need one in the opener. You need the mana to cast the one you draw.

Here is the hand that loses games: two punishers and no engine. Iron Maiden charges hand size minus four and Ebony Owl Netsuke needs seven cards, so against a table drawing one card a turn both of them read "does nothing." Engine plus punisher only assembles by turn six in 41.2% of games. A hand that promises the lock without holding half of it is a mulligan wearing a costume. Ship it.

Never mulligan toward the kill either. Four named cards is not a keepable target — win-condition access shows up by turn six in only 50.5% of games, and Enlightened Tutor and Long-Term Plans are what fetch the missing piece in the midgame. Keep the hand that plays turns two through five well and let the deck find the rest.

The keep you should be greedier about is the cheap tax. Mystic Remora on one or Rhystic Study on two turns a fair opener into a great one, and Kwain and Kami both count as engines at two mana. Free counters are the exception to the rule: Fierce Guardianship needs Heliod on the battlefield, so it is not interaction in an opening hand — it is interaction on turn five.
upgrades:
Ten names, and not one of them moves the bracket: floor 4 before, floor 4 after, on every single entry. That is the signal to read first. This is not a list reaching for more power — it is a list buying certainty around machines that already work, and seven of the ten are sitting in the sideboard rather than out in the market.

Mana Vault is the entry the rest of the list leans on. The verified loop's ledger is three mana spent, three produced per cycle — dead even — and Vault's own cycle is {1} in and {C}{C}{C} out, which is the only candidate in the pool that changes the sign of that number. Compare the alternatives: Worn Powerstone costs 3 to cast, enters tapped and taps for 2; Brass Infiniscope costs 4 and taps for 2. Both run the ledger the wrong way. The honest caveat is that Vault's line has no walkthrough on the record yet — the arithmetic points somewhere, and the arithmetic is not a ruling.

The play-rate spread on these ten is enormous and it maps cleanly onto how conditional they are. Fellwar Stone sits at EDHREC rank 17 and Windfall at 154; Sphinx of the Final Word sits at 10,178, a spread of roughly 600x. The cheap consensus cards are the ones that improve any draw. The four-figure names are answers to a specific table, which is why every one of them carries a condition line — on this list, when is as load-bearing as what.

Two entries come with an obsolescence flag, and both flags die on the oracle text. The index proposes Super-Adaptoid over Sphinx of the Final Word at 0.8848 similarity, and Syncopate over No More Lies at 0.9971 — a near-perfect match on a card that neither exiles nor taxes at a fixed rate. That is a useful demonstration of what a similarity score measures and where it stops: two counterspells can look identical to the model and do different jobs at the table.
mana_base:
Thirty-three lands across 18 entries, and seven of them enter tapped — but only two do so unconditionally. Karsten's cap on pure taplands is about four before you rethink the base, so at Temple of Enlightenment and Irrigated Farmland you are comfortably under it. The other five negotiate: Glacial Fortress wants a Plains or Island, Prairie Stream wants two basics, Deserted Beach and Seachrome Coast key off your land count from opposite directions, and Hallowed Fountain just charges 2 life.

The colour split is where the interesting disagreement lives. Blue carries 79.2% of the pip load — 61 pips across 40 cards — on 63.4% of the sources. White carries 20.8%, or 16 pips across 14 cards, on 36.6%. On paper white is over-sourced by a wide margin. In practice it isn't taking anything from blue: 11 of the 15 white land sources tap for blue as well, and the only white-only mana in the deck is three Plains and Eiganjo.

On curve, off lands alone, you make white 78.7% of the time and blue 74.2%. Rocks and dorks lift that to 88.1% and 83.9%. The 90% yardstick wants 36 blue sources and 22 white; you have 26 and 15 in lands, 31 and 20 counting everything. The audit says the quiet part out loud — that target is a yardstick, not a possibility, in a 33-land deck. It is priced off a 40-land build casting on curve, and this deck is neither.

Six rocks, one ritual and three cost-reducers cover the gap, and they buy two different things. Arcane Signet, Azorius Signet and Talisman of Progress buy colour; Sol Ring and Thought Vessel buy only generic; Smothering Tithe buys Treasures off a table you are actively making draw. Watch the handoff in the goldfish log: land-drop hit rate falls from 86.6% on turn three to 72.5% on four to 47.1% by six, while mean available mana keeps climbing — 4.12, then 5.325, then 7.033 by turn ten. Past turn four, the rocks are the mana base.

One last reason the yardstick reads harsh here. It prices every cast at sticker, and this deck rarely pays sticker: the Warped Eclipse takes {1} off per card your opponents drew this turn. What a discount cannot reach is a coloured pip. Blue's effective pip load is 2 with a maximum of 3, and that maximum is Archmage's Charm — a card Karsten's table wants 37 sources for against the 31 you have.
